title: xAI ships Grok 4.6 for long-running agents at half the frontier price
subtitle: The new flagship reuses the Grok 4.5 base, matches GPT-5.6 Sol on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, and lists at $2 per million input tokens.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: xAI released Grok 4.6 on August 12, 2026, positioning it as a flagship model tuned for long-running agent work — multi-step research, cross-repository coding, and turning briefs into finished artifacts. The company kept the 1.5-trillion-parameter base from Grok 4.5 (which shipped five weeks earlier) and spent the release cycle on supervised fine-tuning over regenerated trajectories plus wide-ranging reinforcement learning across engineering and domain-specific environments. The model ships with a 500,000-token context window and a February 1, 2026 knowledge cutoff, and it is available the same day through the xAI API, in Cursor, and in xAI's own Grok Build tool.

The pricing is the sharper signal. Grok 4.6 lists at $2 per million input tokens and $6 per million output tokens — roughly half of what OpenAI and Anthropic charge for the frontier tier they claim to match. xAI says Grok 4.6 ties GPT-5.6 Sol on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, a nine-benchmark composite, and trades leads with GPT-5.6 Sol and Anthropic's Fable 5 across the other public evals. For the first week, xAI is doubling included usage in Grok Build and Cursor to accelerate adoption.

The context here is the reused-base pattern that showed up first with GPT-5.6 Sol/Luna and now with Grok 4.5/4.6 — labs are getting more mileage from a single pretraining run by pushing gains into post-training and RL rather than starting from scratch. That is the same pattern that took Anthropic from Claude Sonnet 5 to Fable 5 and OpenAI from GPT-5.5 to GPT-5.6. The frontier isn't converging on capability parity so much as on a release rhythm: one heavy base per year, then rolling upgrades every four to six weeks.

A note for learners: when a lab prices a frontier-claim model at half the rate of its rivals, watch the second-order effect on the API market rather than the leaderboard. Cheaper frontier tokens make agent workflows — where thousands of tokens per task are normal — economically viable for cases that were previously priced out. If you build with LLMs, the interesting question this week isn't 'which model is best?' — it's 'which workloads become buildable once the input token cost drops below $3?'
